subject: technology
topic: Your phone weakens your thinking even when you are not using it
angle: Some studies find that a smartphone’s mere presence can reduce working‑memory capacity or lower attention, but other large meta‑analyses find no significant effect, leaving the evidence mixed.
title: phone presence and focus

hooks.text: Do phones really pull your focus?
Phones sit idle but may still cost your memory.
You might be losing attention when your phone is near.
A charger on the table and a quiet kitchen.
Phones and attention: the evidence is mixed.

reveal.headline: A phone nearby can lower working memory
reveal.body: The mere presence of a smartphone reduces available cognitive capacity.

explain.headline: What the evidence shows
explain.body: Some experiments report small negative impacts of a phone’s presence on cognition. Larger meta‑analyses find no reliable effect. The evidence is mixed.

matters.headline: Why you might notice
matters.body: That may be why you feel less focus when a phone sits nearby, even if you do not look at it.

example.headline: A quiet morning in the kitchen
example.body: You are reading the news on your phone while a charger sits on the counter. The phone stays off, but you notice it more than the article.

question.headline: Do you feel distracted by phones around you?

stat.label: effect of phone presence on cognition

claims.text: The mere presence of smartphone had no significant effect on cognitive outcomes.
claims.quote: It was found that the mere presence of smartphone had no significant effect on cognitive outcomes (d = −0. 02, SE = 0. 02, 95% CI [−0. 06, 0. 01], p = . 246).

claims.text: Working memory capacity was negatively impacted by the mere presence of a smartphone.
claims.quote: Working memory capacity was negatively impacted by the mere presence of a smartphone, while results for the remaining cognitive functions produced null summary effects.

claims.text: Participants with higher positive urgency presented increased cognitive interference in the "silent-mode smartphone" condition compared with participants in the "turned-off smartphone" condition.
claims.quote: participants with higher positive urgency presented increased cognitive interference (reflected by poorer task performance) in the "silent-mode smartphone" condition compared with participants in the "turned-off smartphone" condition.

claims.text: The mere presence of a smartphone results in lower cognitive performance, which supports the hypothesis of the smartphone presence using limited cognitive resources.
claims.quote: The results of the conducted experiment imply that the mere presence of a smartphone results in lower cognitive performance, which supports the hypothesis of the smartphone presence using limited cognitive resources.

claims.text: The mere presence of one’s own smartphone reduces available cognitive capacity.
claims.quote: The mere presence of one’s own smartphone may occupy limited-capacity cognitive resources, thereby leaving fewer resources available for other tasks and undercutting cognitive performance.

claims.text: The model further suggests a quantification of smartphone usage based on different quantitative parameters, such as usage time, usage frequency, used applications, and received notifications.

verdict: The evidence shows that the effect of a smartphone’s mere presence on cognition is inconsistent: a few experiments report small negative impacts, while larger meta‑analyses find no reliable effect.
caveat: The conclusions are limited by methodological heterogeneity, small sample sizes in some experiments, and the fact that many studies rely on observational or short‑term laboratory tasks that may not reflect real‑world use.
caption: A phone near you can reduce working‑memory capacity, according to experiments. Larger meta‑analyses find no reliable effect. The evidence is mixed. Do you notice a difference when a phone sits in sight?
